newsitem.title: INDIA: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - February 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - February 17.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for Reuters by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3324842, 3351006, 3761233 Fax:+91-11-3351006 Internet: biznis@giasbm01.vsnl.net.in
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
The Pioneer
23 SLAIN IN TRIPURA

The Disturbed Areas Act was imposed in six trouble-torn areas of west Tripura. Shoot-at-sight orders were issued to the army and para-military forces after militants killed 23 non-tribals. In a fresh outbreak of violence, hundreds of houses were torched in different parts of the curfew-bound areas of the state while nine persons were killed in a militant raid. Sources said armed militants attacked a residential area on Saturday night and killed 15 non-tribals besides setting several houses ablaze.
Indian Express
LEFT HARDLINERS WANT TO OPPOSE ECONOMIC POLICIES

Hardliners in the Marxist Communist Party (CPM) took control of the proceedings in the party's central committee meeting. They accused West Bengal chief minister Jyoti Basu of violating party principles and wanted the CPM to distance itself from the ruling United Front. Basu was criticised for suggesting that his chances of becoming prime minister were sabotaged by people who did not like him. The CPM hawks also stressed for the party to increase its opposition to the government's economic policies.
The Times Of India
CONGRESS TO GIVE ISSUE-BASED SUPPORT

The Congress Working Committee (CWC) resolved to extend issue-based support to the United Front (UF) government. This was in contrast to its earlier stand of giving unconditional support. The CWC also authorised the party president to talk to the UF constituents and take appropriate steps. This shift in the party's stand was interpreted in political circles as the Congress's first step towards withdrawing support to the Deve Gowda government.
The Economic Times
LIMIT ON INTER-CORPORATE LOANS, INVESTMENTS PROPOSED

Companies would be allowed to invest up to 60 percent of their net worth in shares and loans of other companies compared to only 30 percent each in the present Companies Act. In addition, buybacks and non-voting shares would be allowed and company boards would be given greater powers. These were some of the salient features of the draft Companies Bill, 1997.
NAGARJUNA, CHAMBAL SUBSIDY RAISED

The Fertiliser Ministry decided to increase the subsidy to Chambal Fertilisers and Nagarjuna Fertilisers. This followed a decision by the ministry to permit capitalisation of the actual rate of interest, pegged at 20 percent, paid by Chambal and Nagarjuna Fertilisers while calculating their final retention price. Until now, the government has refused to accept these interest costs as part of the final subsidy to be paid to these fertiliser units.
ESSAR TO SELL TAMILNADU MERCANTILE BANK

The Essar group would sell off its entire 69 percent stake in the Tamilnadu Mercantile Bank to Dubai-based C. Sivasankaran and his family members, former owners of Sterling Computers. The group's decision to get out of the bank stemmed from the central bank's refusal to transfer the shares in its name on the grounds that current rules did not allow large private industrial groups to own or control banks.
Financial Express
KOEL -KARO, CHAMERA PROJECTS MAY BE SHELVED

The National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC) was likely to shelve two politically sensitive hydro-electric schemes, Koel-Karo in Bihar and Chamera II in Himachal Pradesh, because of their high project cost. The fund-starved NHPC was toying with the idea of scrapping the two unviable schemes for sometime now. While the Bihar chief minister was egging on the government to part with funds for the 24 billion rupee Koel-Karo project, the power minister was all for the 28.5 billion rupee Chamera II. In both cases NHPC held that the cost of electricity would be so high as to be unreasonable and it would be difficult to get customers at such heavy rate.
Business Standard
INDIA SIGNS TELECOMMUNICATION PACT

India signed a global telecommunications pact, along with 67 other countries, at a World Trade Organisation meeting in Geneva. Under the accord, signatory nations would open up long-protected telecom monopolies to competition from both foreign and domestic firms, based on their commitments made at the talks. India retained a binding commitment of 25 percent foreign equity in telecom service companies in its offer. Earlier, there were indications that it would increase its offer to 49 percent foreign.
LEFT FOR MINIMUM TAX ON GROSS PROFITS

The Communist Party (Marxist) (CPM) wants the minimum alternate tax (MAT) to remain next year. Party leaders said the present system of asking companies to pay taxes on the basis of book profits left too many loopholes. A senior CPM member suggested charging MAT on gross profits and not on book profits. The dual accounting procedure, sanctioned by differing methodology under the Companies act and Income Tax Act, enables companies to show profits to stockholders and yet rely on a no-tax liability by taking advantage of depreciation provisions and other tax set-offs.
ESSAR PLANS $1.13 BLN BORROWINGS FOR EXPANSION

The 25 billion rupee steel, oil, telecommunication and power conglomerate Essar group was planning external commercial borrowings (ECBs) of about $1.13 billion to repay high-cost debt and finance expansion. Essar Commvison, the holder of the letter of intent for basic telecom services in Punjab, will make an ECB offering of $350 million, Essar Oil $330 million, cellular telecom firm Sterling Cellular $175 million, group flagship Essar Steel $140 million and Essar Power $138 million.
MAJOR BOOST FOR SERVICE EXPORTS LIKELY IN EXIM POLICY

Service exports, including tourism, legal service, medical services, health consultancy and software, were likely to receive significant benefits in the new Export-Import (Exim) policy covering the next five years. The director-general of foreign trade said it was possible that these sectors would be allowed a higher level of duty-free imports.
NEW NORMS FOR UNCLAIMED DIVIDENDS LIKELY

Companies may no longer be required to transfer unclaimed dividends to the general revenue account of the government. Instead, they would have to deposit the unpaid amount in a special bank account within 37 days. This was among the changes being proposed by the working group set up to recast the Companies Act, relating to norms governing the declaration of dividend and its utilisation.
The Observer
GOVERNEMNT STAFF THREATENS UNITED STIR

Representatives of various associations of government employees and workers warned the government of collective agitation if their grievances, coming in the wake of the Fifth Pay Commission report, were not redressed. This was the first time these representatives came together and were speaking at a collective platform since the Pay Panel report came out.
FINANCE MINISTRY WANTS LIST OF DEFAULTERS

The Finance Ministry asked banks to prepare a comprehensive list of importers who defaulted in submitting bills of entry (BOE) on stipulated time to the banks in the last five years. BOE was the most essential document which verified the actual outgo of foreign exchange towards imports. The ministry was reported to have sufficient grounds to believe that a section of importers had despatched foreign exchange worth billions of rupees through illegal transfers.
SLOWDOWN IN INDUSTRIAL GROWTH BOTTOMS OUT CMIE

The industrial sector posted robust growth rates in December 1996 after the disappointing performance of November 1996. Despite the low growth in November 1996, according to a Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy study there were signs in the preliminary estimates of December 1996 that the slowdown in industrial growth had bottomed out. The weighted average of the growth in output of a large number of industries (accounting for about 60 percent of the weight in the official index of industrial production) was a meagre two percent compared to the 4.2 percent increase recorded in October 1996.
Business Line
VOLUME-LINKED CAPITAL NORMS FOR INSURERS LIKELY

The norms for capital requirements of private insurance firms in the post-liberalised set-up was likely to be linked to the volume of business transacted by the company. Finance Ministry officials said the Insurance Regulatory Authority and the government were considering outlining a graded pattern for capitalisation of the companies, keeping in view the amount of business handled by them. However, no exact formula had emerged in this regard yet.
